text.p: Plans by steel wire and cord maker Bekaert NV to lay off workers in its native Belgium but open a factory in Indonesia were criticised on Monday by a leading human rights activist.

Jose Ramos-Horta, whose campaign against Indonesia's 1975 military annexation of East Timor was recognised in the form of a Nobel Peace Prize in 1996, said Bekaert's move was an example of how western companies had been seduced by cheap Asian labour.
"These companies only shift production because of slave conditions in (Indonesia) where workers earn $1 to $3 for a 15-hour day," Horta told a news conference at the Belgian Parliament.
"Asian countries are competing in who has the cheapest labour... It is why you are losing jobs in Belgium, Europe and the U.S.," Horta added.
Horta was speaking after meeting European Union Commission President Jacques Santer at the start of a three-day visit to Brussels to address Belgian and EU politicians.

Bekaert announced plans to invest $20 million in a steel cord plant near Jakarta last July. Job cuts in Europe were announced earlier this year, when the company also criticised Belgium's high labour costs.

"Bekaert decided last week to close a factory in Belgium with the loss of 200 jobs at the same time as opening in Indonesia, which is a dictatorship where human rights go under foot," Belgian member of parliament Lode Vanoost said.
A company spokesman was not immediately available to comment on or confirm Vanoost's remark.
Horta said the struggle for democracy and human rights in Asian nations and western economic interests were linked and did not have to remain opposed.
"If there's rule of law and workers rights it means dictatorships won't be able to pay dollar-a-day for goods made cheaper than elsewhere," Horta said.

Horta said, however, he did not believe in blanket economic sanctions as a means to punish regimes. "We believe that economic engagement with a country can at times foster positive changes through the development of a democratically conscious middle class," he said.
